title: Functions, arguments, and lifetimes
objective: By the end of this lesson you can write and declare functions correctly, and you can explain how long each kind of variable lives — which is the idea the rest of the course depends on.

blocks.caption: Declaration, definition, call
lines: int add(int a, int b);            /* declaration: the signature, no body */
int add(int a, int b) {           /* definition: the actual code */

blocks.title: Declaration and definition are separate on purpose
blocks.text: The declaration tells the compiler the shape of the function so it can check your calls. The definition provides the code, and the linker matches the two. That separation is what lets a project be split across files — and it is also why a missing definition surfaces as 'undefined reference' at link time rather than as a compile error.

blocks.caption: The function gets a copy
lines: void really_change(int *n) {      /* pass the address instead */

blocks.text: There is no exception to this rule. When you pass a pointer, the pointer itself is copied — but the copy holds the same address, so the function can reach the original. This is the whole mechanism behind output parameters, and it is why the next module is the heart of the course.
Lifetime: how long a variable exists

rows: The program exits — value persists between calls

blocks.caption: static keeps its value between calls
lines: static int count = 0;    /* initialised once, not on every call */

blocks.title: Never return the address of a local variable
blocks.text: A local variable ceases to exist when the function returns, so a pointer to it points at reclaimed stack space. The program may appear to work — the value is often still sitting there untouched — until another call reuses that memory and the value silently changes. This is one of the most common serious mistakes in early C, and -Wall catches the obvious form of it.

blocks.caption: The wrong way and two right ways
lines: return buf;              /* WRONG: buf is gone when this returns */
void caller_provides(char *out, size_t n) {   /* caller owns the memory */
char *heap_version(void) {   /* or allocate; caller must free */

blocks.text: static at file level means 'private to this file'

blocks.caption: Two meanings, one keyword
lines: static int helper(int x) { ... }   /* not visible to other files */
int public_api(int x) { ... }      /* visible to the whole program */

blocks.text: Inside a function, static means 'keep the value between calls'. At file level, it means 'do not export this name'. The second use is how C limits what a file exposes, and marking everything internal as static is a cheap way to keep a module's surface small.

blocks.caption: The C convention: return status, write results through pointers

blocks.title: Check every return value, every time
blocks.text: C has no exceptions. A function that can fail tells you by its return value, and a caller that ignores it continues with a value that was never set. Most memory-corruption stories start with an unchecked malloc, an unchecked fopen, or an unchecked parse.

blocks.title: Watch lifetime and pass-by-value in action
steps: Write try_to_change and really_change from above; print x after each call
Write the counter() function with static and call it three times
Write the broken() function that returns a local buffer; compile with -Wall and read the warning
Run it anyway and see what it prints — then call another function before printing, and compare
Rewrite it as caller_provides() and confirm the output is stable
With Clang, compile with -fsanitize=address -fsanitize-address-use-after-return=always and run the broken version again
blocks.expected: A copy that does not affect the original, a pointer that does, a static counter that remembers, and a returned local buffer that appears to work until something else uses the stack. With the explicit Clang use-after-return mode, AddressSanitizer reports stack-use-after-return.

cheatsheet: Declaration = signature (checks calls); definition = code (linker matches them)
C passes everything by value — pass an address to let a function modify the original
Local variables live on the stack and die when the function returns
static inside a function: value persists between calls
static at file level: the name is private to that file
Never return a pointer to a local variable
Either the caller provides the buffer, or you allocate and document who frees it
Convention: return 0 or a status code, write results through pointer parameters
Check every return value — C has no exceptions to fall back on

checkpoint.prompt: You pass an int to a function and it assigns a new value to the parameter. What happens to the caller's variable?
checkpoint.explanation: The function received a copy. To modify the caller's variable you pass its address and write through the pointer.

checkpoint.prompt: Why must you never return a pointer to a local variable?

choices.B: The local dies when the function returns
choices.C: Local variables cannot be addressed at all

checkpoint.explanation: The pointer refers to reclaimed stack memory that another call will overwrite. It often appears to work at first, because the value is still sitting in memory nobody has reused yet — which is what makes it dangerous.

checkpoint.prompt: What does static mean on a variable declared inside a function?

choices.A: It is visible to other files through the linker
choices.B: It keeps its value between calls
choices.D: It is stored on the stack

checkpoint.explanation: At file level the same keyword means something different: the name is not exported to other files.

checkpoint.prompt: What is the standard C convention for a function that can fail?

choices.C: Return the result and print errors to the screen
choices.D: Return status; write the result through a pointer

checkpoint.explanation: The caller can check before using it. There are no exceptions in C. The status return is the only signal, and an unchecked one means continuing with a value that was never set.
